S1.cite: Mudare S., Jing J., Makowski D., et al. (2025). Crop rotations synergize yield, nutrition, and revenue: a meta-analysis. Nature Communications 16, 9552.
S1.finding: 3,663 paired field observations from 738 experiments (1980-2024): legume pre-crops raised the following crop's yield by 23% on average versus 16% for non-legume pre-crops; whole rotation sequences gave 14-27% more yield, dietary energy, protein, iron, magnesium, zinc and revenue than continuous monoculture; yields varied less from year to year.

S2.cite: Franke A.C., van den Brand G.J., Vanlauwe B., Giller K.E. (2018). Systematic review of grain-legume rotations with cereals in sub-Saharan Africa (44 publications, 199 observations).
S2.finding: All grain legumes improved cereal yields; effects were stronger after soybean and groundnut than after cowpea, and stronger for maize than for millet and sorghum.

S3.cite: Bagayoko M., Buerkert A., Lung G., Bationo A., Roemheld V. (2000). Cereal/legume rotation effects on cereal growth in Sudano-Sahelian West Africa. Plant and Soil 218:103-116.
S3.finding: Cereal yields rose after legumes at all four sites; soil mineral nitrogen effects were larger after groundnut than cowpea; sorghum after groundnut had fewer nematodes, but millet and cowpea were both good nematode hosts.

S4.cite: FAO (1986) seasonal crop water needs, as tabulated by SSWM (Crop Selection factsheet).
S4.finding: Approximate seasonal water needs in mm: bean 300-500, maize 500-800, peanut 500-700, rice (paddy) 450-700, sorghum/millet 450-650, soybean 450-700, wheat 450-650.

S5.cite: University of Nebraska CropWatch (2020), summarising Gentry et al. (2013) and Seifert et al.: Yield penalties for continuous corn and soybean in the Midwest, US.
S5.finding: Continuous corn averaged a 4.3% yield penalty and continuous soybean 10.3% versus rotated crops, larger in low-moisture and low-yield conditions.

S6.cite: China crop-rotation meta-analysis (45 studies, 214 comparisons), record 19654813 on peeref.
S6.finding: Rotation benefits were much larger at low nitrogen rates (120 kg/ha or less) and persisted for 2-3 years; legume pre-crops gave the largest gains.

S7.cite: FAO and IIASA (2025). Global Agro-ecological Zoning v5 (GAEZ v5) model documentation.
S7.finding: Suitability compares attainable yield with the maximum biological yield for the crop; seven suitability classes from highly suitable to unsuitable, separately for rain-fed or irrigated water supply and low or high input management.

S8.cite: Global systematic review with meta-analysis reveals yield advantage of legume-based rotations and its drivers. Nature Communications 13 (2022).
S8.finding: Legume-based rotations raised yields by 20.4% on average across 462 experiments in 53 countries; about a quarter of observations were negative; the effect was smaller with high nitrogen input or high diversity and larger in low-yielding settings.

S9.cite: Yao et al. (2025). Legume-rice rotations. One Earth.
S9.finding: Rice yield rose by 15.7% after legumes, with larger gains under low nitrogen input.
